questions.question: A policy excels in simulation but fails on real messiness it never saw. What bridges that gap?
options: More simulation of the same clean kind
Trust in simulation scores alone
No evaluation before deployment
Noise-robust training plus realistic evals
questions.explanation: Clean training meets messy reality. This lesson transfers with slip modeled and proven.

questions.question: What is the training-environment difference between train_fixed(0.0) and train_dr(0.0, 0.3)?
options: The fixed run uses Monte Carlo while DR uses a policy gradient
The fixed run keeps slip at 0.0, whereas DR samples one slip value uniformly in [0.0, 0.3] for each episode
The fixed run has no epsilon exploration, while DR has epsilon=1.0
The fixed run trains on a 4x4 grid and DR on a 5x5 grid
questions.explanation: train_fixed passes its slip unchanged; train_dr calls rng.uniform(slip_low, slip_high) once per episode before collecting the trajectory.

questions.question: Which slip values are sampled by train_dr(slip_low=0.0, slip_high=0.3)?
options: Only 0.0 and 0.3, alternating every step
A value above 0.7 for every training episode
One uniform random value between 0.0 and 0.3 per episode, reused for that episode's steps
A new value chosen from ACTIONS for every state
questions.explanation: The function samples slip_ep before the episode loop and passes that same episode parameter to every step in the rollout.

questions.question: How does evaluate choose actions for a learned Q table?
options: It samples uniformly from ACTIONS regardless of Q
It uses epsilon=0.15 to keep exploring on hardware
It averages all four action values before moving
It takes max(ACTIONS, key=lambda a: Q[s][a]) with no exploration
questions.explanation: evaluate is a greedy test: at each state it chooses the action with the largest stored Q value and only the slip remains stochastic.

questions.question: How does main label its evaluation table for slips 0.0 through 0.7?
options: Slips at or below 0.3 are in-support for DR; larger slips are marked OOD for DR
Every slip is marked in-support because evaluation never changes the simulator
Only slip=0.7 is in-support because it is the hardest case
The fixed policy's training slip determines all labels
questions.explanation: The printed label checks `slip <= 0.3`, matching the domain-randomization training envelope [0.0,0.3].

questions.question: What trade-off does the lesson associate with overly broad domain randomization?
options: It guarantees a policy that is optimal for every possible robot
A policy can become overly cautious because excessive variation acts like strong regularization
It removes the need for any real-world evaluation
It makes the simulator deterministic and eliminates the reality gap by definition
questions.explanation: The docs note that excessive noise can produce a universal but timid policy; the randomization envelope should cover plausible reality without drowning the signal.
